newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris court clears U.S. school on English website.
newsitem.headline: Paris court clears U.S. school on English website.

text.p: The first test of whether France's disputed language law applies to the Internet ended in fiasco on Monday when a court threw out the case on a technicality.
Two state-approved watchdogs promoting the use of the French language had filed a complaint against the U.S. Georgia Institute of Technology's French campus for using English only on its website.
The plaintiffs, Defence of the French Language and Future of the French Language, accused Georgia Tech Lorraine of breaking a 1994 law requiring all advertising in France to be in French.
The Paris police court dismissed the suit, saying the two private groups should have notified a public prosecutor first.
The legislation, named after then culture minister Jacques Toubon, was part of a long-running battle to protect the tongue of Moliere and Racine from the growing global grip of English.

"The central question, the most interesting one, has not been decided today, only a procedural matter has," said Marc Jobert, lawyer for the two groups, which had demanded that the Internet site be translated into French.

While Internet champions say the worldwide web should be free of national restraints, many governments have asserted their authority over cyberspace to try to block pornography or silence political dissent.
"The court did not address the underlying issue and has left us wanting more," said Jacques Schaefer, lawyer for Georgia Tech Lorraine, based in Metz, eastern France.
"It's a total victory in the sense that we were cleared of all accusations," he said, but the university would rather have won on substance than on procedure.
Georgia Tech president Wayne Clough said the drive to apply the Toubon law to the web ignores its "interconnected nature".
"The Web is the personification of the much-touted global economy. It does not recognise national or linguistic borders," he said.

Georgia Tech argued at a January hearing that communications on the web were like telephone calls. It said its website was in English because all its courses were taught in the language of Shakespeare and students were required to be fluent in English.

Ironically, two weeks ago, Georgia Tech Lorraine made its website available in French and German as well, but denied the lawsuit was the reason. It said technological advances in the global computer network had made it easier to provide the translation and that it "wanted to be more European".
The two watchdog associations have 10 days to appeal.

Criticised abroad as cultural arrogance and a vain attempt to regulate human conduct by decree, the Toubon law aimed to make the public use of words such as "cheeseburger" and "airbag" punishable by up to six months in prison.
Its scope was limited to advertising by the Constitutional Council, which ruled that its wider provisions had violated the French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man.

The law was music to the ears of many conservatives, but most academics, scientists and artists ridiculed it. Toubon became the butt of jokes even among fellow ministers, who nicknamed him "Mr Allgood", the English translation of his name.
Mickey Mouse was the law's first victim in 1995, when a court condemned a Disney store in Paris for failing to label 10 types of toys with safety advice in French beside the English labels.
